prompt_topic: sacubitril/valsartan (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition) in heart failure
raw_text:
**Introduction and Mechanism of Action**
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, historically treated by targeting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). However, the discovery of the natriuretic peptide system and its cardioprotective actions—such as vasodilation, natriuresis, and anti-fibrotic properties—prompted the development of novel therapeutic pathways. Sacubitril/valsartan is a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) combining the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan in a 1:1 molecular ratio. Neprilysin is responsible for degrading natriuretic peptides; its inhibition, therefore, raises their levels. Crucially, because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, its inhibition requires concurrent block of the angiotensin receptor to prevent severe vasoconstriction. 

**Clinical Evidence in HFrEF**
The clinical treatment of HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was redefined by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. In this double-blind trial, 8,442 chronic HFrEF patients were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril on top of standard therapy. Sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, and a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [1]. Subanalyses confirmed that these clinical benefits were consistent across age groups [2] and that sacubitril/valsartan significantly delayed clinical progression compared to enalapril [3]. The therapy was also shown to remain highly effective in patients unable to tolerate maximum doses, with therapeutic benefit preserved at lower doses [4]. Projections from trial data suggest that transitioning to comprehensive disease-modifying regimens including ARNI therapy translates to significant additions to estimated lifetime survival [5].

**In-Hospital Initiation and Biomarker Progression**
The safety and efficacy of initiating sacubitril/valsartan in hospitalized patients with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) were subsequently addressed. The PIONEER-HF trial randomized stabilized ADHF patients to receive sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril, demonstrating a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels over 8 weeks [6] and a reduction in serious clinical events [7]. Similarly, the TRANSITION trial confirmed that early initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in the hospital or shortly after discharge was highly feasible and well-tolerated [8]. Real-world evidence has corroborated these findings, showing that early initiation reduces post-discharge rehospitalization rates [9].

Mechanistically, this clinical benefit is closely linked to cardiac reverse remodeling. In the PROVE-HF trial, sacubitril/valsartan therapy was associated with rapid, sustained reductions in NT-proBNP that correlated directly with improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and cardiac volumes [10]. The EVALUATE-HF trial expanded on this, showing that although change in aortic impedance did not meet statistical significance compared to enalapril, treatment resulted in a substantial decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volume indices [11]. Further analyses of ambulatory patient biomarker profiles highlighted the stabilization of myocardial wall stress and cardiac injury markers [12], which carries critical prognostic implications for predicting long-term survival and clinical stability [13].

**Extending Efficacy Across Ejection Fraction**
In the phase II PARAMOUNT trial, sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated superior reduction in NT-proBNP compared to valsartan in patients with HF and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [14]. The subsequent phase III PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4,822 patients with LVEF ≥45% to sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan [15]. Although sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint (rate ratio 0.87, p=0.06), substantial benefit was seen in prespecified subgroups, specifically patients with lower ejection fraction (45–57%, corresponding to HF with mildly reduced EF [HFmrEF]) and women [15]. A combined analysis of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF populations demonstrated a continuous clinical benefit of sacubitril/valsartan extending up to an ejection fraction of approximately 55–60% [16]. These findings were reinforced by the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, which proved that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduces NT-proBNP in stabilized acute decompensated patients with LVEF >40% [17].

**Clinical Boundaries and Safety Concerns**
Despite its successes, clinical limitations have been observed. In advanced (NYHA Class IV) HFrEF, the LIFE trial showed no significant improvement in NT-proBNP or clinical outcomes over valsartan [18]. Similarly, in acute myocardial infarction patients without pre-existing HF, the PARADISE-MI trial failed to demonstrate a superior clinical outcome of sacubitril/valsartan over ramipril [19]. Conversely, the pediatric PANORAMA-HF trial confirmed the clinical utility and safety of sacubitril/valsartan in children with HFrEF [20]. To address concerns over potential cognitive impairment due to cerebral amyloid accumulation (as neprilysin degrades amyloid-beta), the PERSPECTIVE trial evaluated cognitive function in patients on sacubitril/valsartan, confirming no adverse impact on cognitive outcomes compared to valsartan [21]. This stands in contrast to historic dual ACE-neprilysin inhibitors like omapatrilat, which were abandoned in trials like OVERTURE due to intolerable angioedema risk [22].

**Cardiorenal Protection and Implementation**
Cardiorenal syndrome remains a frequent complication. In PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan slowed the rate of renal decline and led to lower rates of renal deterioration compared to enalapril [23]. This renal protection was similarly observed in the PARAGON-HF cohort [24] and further validated in patients with chronic kidney disease in the UK HARP-III trial [25]. Furthermore, patients treated with sacubitril/valsartan had a lower risk of severe hyperkalemia compared to those receiving enalapril [26].

Based on this body of evidence, both the ESC [27] and AHA/ACC/HFSA [28] clinical guidelines recommend sacubitril/valsartan as Class I first-line therapy for HFrEF. However, the CHAMP-HF registry has highlighted a persistent implementation gap in real-world practice, with many eligible patients remaining untreated or under-dosed [29]. Addressing this implementation gap is critical, given that optimization of ARNI therapy is highly cost-effective and improves overall clinical outcomes [30].
